beats.say: In 997, a youthful Mahmud of Ghazni swore secret allegiance to the rising warlord Muhammad Ghori.
They forged a covert pact to split the rich Indian plains, promising each half of loot.
When Mahmud stormed Somnath in 1025, he secretly diverted a portion of the temple's gold to Ghori's army.
Ghori used that treasure to fund his 1192 conquest of Delhi, buying cavalry from Central Asian mercenaries.
The alliance stayed hidden because chroniclers feared portraying the famed invaders as collaborators.
Modern historians note the sudden surge of horse-archer tactics in Ghori's forces mirrors Mahmud's cavalry style.

beats.say: A 13th-century Persian manuscript even lists a joint treasury entry dated 1193, confirming shared spoils.
This covert bond explains why Ghori's empire expanded swiftly while Mahmud's campaigns dwindled after 1030.
The hidden pact reshaped South Asian power maps, paving the way for the Delhi Sultanate's rise.
So the legend of two lone conquerors is really a story of a whispered partnership.
